mappings.note: What rock paintings let us infer - the paintings are the source (LO-59) and the inference is about early humans' hunting, beliefs and artistry (LO-62). The item asks for both, so both are cited.
The warming after the Ice Age leading people to settle, cultivate and domesticate - the broad development LO-63 names. Not LO-62, which covers cultural features rather than this transition.
Why early farmers chose riversides: water and fertile land at the start of agriculture, squarely LO-63. Not LO-57, no Indian river is located.
Defines what a historian is and does. No outcome defines the practitioner; LO-59 is about the sources, so the goal is the honest altitude, as with the definition of History itself.
Fossils as preserved remains studied by palaeontology - the evidence base for the deep past, so LO-59 rather than an early-human-culture outcome.
The Gregorian leap-year rule, including the divisible-by-400 exception for century years; a mechanism of the dating framework, hence LO-65.
What monuments reveal about architecture, belief and power - the 'describe their use' clause of LO-59 applied to structures. Not LO-60, since nothing is placed on a map.
Belief in an afterlife among early humans - a distinctive feature of their culture. Not LO-59: the question asks what they believed, not how we know it.
Defines domestication of animals, part of the beginning of agriculture that LO-63 names alongside cultivation.
How pottery served settled communities through storage, cooking and transport; asked from the settled-life side, so LO-63 rather than LO-62, which is used where pottery is named only as an invention.

Welfare as the chieftain's responsibility for the group - leadership and social organisation in early communities, which LO-62 covers. This is the substantive version of the bare glossary item on 'welfare', which was left unmapped because it names no historical content at all.

E. H. Carr's dialogue between present and past, and why history matters: a statement about the discipline as a whole, which only the goal reaches. LO-59 concerns sources and LO-65 chronology, neither of which is being tested.
Explains BCE/CE, why it was adopted and how to span a BCE date to a CE one allowing for the absent year zero - the fullest chronology item in the chapter.
The jigsaw analogy: sources are partial, biased or lost, and the historian must still reconstruct. That is exactly LO-59's 'describe their use in the reconstruction of the history'.
Names all four source categories with an example of each and what it reveals - the most complete source-classification item in the chapter, so LO-59.
Climate change at the end of the Ice Age as the enabling condition for agriculture and settlement; the same broad development as the shorter version, at five-mark length.
Fire and tool-making and what they did for survival - the growth of early human culture and technology, which LO-62 asks pupils to explain. Not LO-63, whose developments begin with farming.

Traces bands to hamlets to villages to towns, which is LO-63's arc from hunting-gathering through agriculture towards the first cities; LO-62 is added because the answer also turns on chieftainship and craft, the cultural features of those communities.
Which artefacts an excavator would seek (LO-59) and what each says about diet, technology, status and belief (LO-62). The item is built on the step from evidence to inference, so both are needed.
Ancient art as evidence where writing is absent - a claim about the value of a source type, hence LO-59. Not LO-62: the question is about the method, not about the early people themselves.
Why historians must weigh bias and incompleteness in their sources; the critical-use clause of LO-59 stated in the abstract.

The panchanga's solar and lunar calculations and their tie to festivals and farming is India's contribution in astronomy, which LO-74 names. Not LO-65, because the item is about an Indian knowledge tradition rather than about dating conventions.

Sets Homo sapiens at 300,000 years and writing at 6,500 against the earth's billions - a scale-of-time argument (LO-65) about the human record (LO-62). Distinct from the plain 300,000-year recall item, which took LO-62 alone.

Campsite case: charred bones, stone tools, a hearth and no pottery or metal are read as evidence (LO-59) for a hunter-gatherer Stone Age culture and its cave art (LO-62). The whole item is an inference-from-evidence exercise.
Places the Harappans and Ashoka on a time line and computes the gaps, including years-ago from 2025 CE. Every sub-part is date arithmetic, so LO-65 alone rather than a development outcome.
A merchant's letters and account books against European travelogues, and what to do when they conflict - classification and critical cross-checking of literary sources, all inside LO-59.
Burial case: grave goods and DNA as evidence (LO-59) read for belief in an afterlife, bronze metallurgy and social ranking (LO-62). Mapped like the other excavation-inference items.
